segs: Meet Chidori.
The agent framework where every run is durable, replayable, and resumable, by default.
Agents are non-deterministic, expensive, and long-running.
A bug shows up three runs deep, and you can't reproduce it.
Every debugging cycle re-bills the same tokens.
A crash halfway through loses everything.
And waiting on a human means keeping a process alive for hours.
Most frameworks layer orchestration on top of that chaos. Chidori removes it at the source, with a single boundary.
Every side effect, every LLM call, tool call, and HTTP request, flows through the runtime as a recorded host call.
The runtime sees everything. So it can log it, cache it, replay it, pause on it, and resume from it.
And you write agents as plain, async TypeScript.
No graphs. No D S L. No activity definitions.
Every await on chidori is a durable safepoint.
Under the hood, it's one Rust binary.
Agents run on an embedded, pure Rust JavaScript engine. A bytecode VM with no C and no unsafe code, conformance tested against Test two six two.
Host functions are the only way out to the world, and the call log journals every one of them.
Journals can be mirrored to S3, SQLite, or Durable Objects. No Node. No V8. No native bindings.
Here's the payoff.
Replay any run against its call log, and every prompt and tool call returns its recorded result, instantly.
Zero tokens. Byte-identical output. Because the runtime fixes the clock and seeds randomness.
Kill the process mid-run,
and Chidori resumes exactly where it left off, in a brand new process, by replaying to the pause point and continuing live.
Need a human to approve something? chidori dot input suspends the run to disk.
No process held open. No threads. No memory.
Answer minutes, or days later, and the run picks up right where it stopped.
And any recorded run becomes a test.
Commit the checkpoint, replay it in C I, and assert the agent hasn't drifted.
A full integration test that costs nothing and runs in milliseconds.
So how does it compare?
Graph frameworks, like Lang Graph, give you L L M primitives, but you author node graphs, and durable, zero-cost replay isn't the default.
Durable execution engines, like Temporal, survive crashes, but you bring your own L L M layer, and operate a server, workers, and a queue.
Chidori gives you both. In plain TypeScript. In one binary.
And there's more.
Branching runs. Supervised actors. Detached agents that hibernate at zero cost. Multiplayer signals.
Structural prompt caching. N P M packages without Node. And OpenTelemetry traces that point straight back to a replayable run.
Install it with one command, scaffold an agent, and start building agents you can actually debug.
Chidori. Checkpoint. Replay. Resume.
